extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers seeking an encyclopedic summary of Twitter/X's history, policies, and platform practices
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style article describing Twitter/X's features, governance, policies, technical implementation, and enforcement actions. The page collates platform rules, regulatory interactions, product changes, and examples of enforcement and controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political advertising policy (2019 ban and 2023 reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: In October 2019 Twitter announced it would stop running political ads effective November 22; the company later reversed the ban in August 2023 and published criteria governing political advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 2019 rationale: political ads contained spurious claims; 2023 criteria: political ads 'do not allow the promotion of false or misleading content' and require advertisers to comply with laws, with compliance being the sole responsibility of the advertiser.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate-change advertising restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: In April 2022 Twitter announced a ban on 'misleading' advertisements that go against 'the scientific consensus on climate change'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twitter stated decisions would be made with the help of 'authoritative sources', including the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC); full guidelines were not provided in the announcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising bans for specific foreign state media
rubrics_metrics.description: In October 2017 Twitter banned the Russian media outlets RT and Sputnik from advertising on their website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ban followed conclusions that those outlets had been used as vehicles for interference in the 2016 US presidential election; public diplomatic reactions (e.g., Maria Zakharova) framed it as a free-speech dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising content & compliance responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter's political advertising rules require advertisers to comply with laws and hold compliance as the sole responsibility of the advertiser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reallowing political ads in 2023, Twitter explicitly required legal compliance and prohibited promotion of false or misleading content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blocking URLs that point to malicious or banned external content
rubrics_metrics.description: As of July 30, 2020, Twitter will block URLs in tweets that point to external websites containing malicious content (malware/phishing) as well as content already banned on the platform (hate speech, terrorism, child sexual exploitation, privacy breaches, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users that frequently point to such sites may have their accounts suspended. This measure is intended to prevent bypassing tweet content restrictions by linking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive information security program (FTC settlement requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2010 FTC settlement required Twitter to take a number of steps to secure users' private information, including maintenance of a 'comprehensive information security program' to be independently audited biannually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was the first time the FTC had taken action against a social network for security lapses; the program must be maintained and independently audited every six months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-factor authentication as a security measure
rubrics_metrics.description: In April 2013 Twitter announced two-factor login verification as an added measure against hacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduced after a number of high-profile hacks; presented as an additional protection to reduce account compromise risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bug bounty program and vulnerability disclosure/response
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter runs a bug bounty program to accept reports of security issues; a vulnerability reported through the program (Jan 2022) allowed linking emails and phone numbers to accounts and was subsequently fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twitter initially believed no one exploited the bug, but it was later used to compile and sell a list of over 5.4 million profiles. The bug bounty program is the channel for reporting such issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verified accounts criteria and meaning of verification
rubrics_metrics.description: An account with a 'blue tick' verification badge indicates 'we've been in contact with the person or entity the account is representing and verified that it is approved'. Verification is granted 'if it is determined to be of public interest' and 'does not imply an endorsement'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twitter verified six types of accounts in a 2021 relaunch; for some categories (companies, brands, influential individuals), the existence of a Wikipedia page may be used as a criterion for 'Off Twitter Notability'. Verification policies have later been changed (e.g., inclusion in paid services).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paid verification / Twitter Blue changes to verification
rubrics_metrics.description: After the 2022 takeover, verification was reported to be included in the paid Twitter Blue service and existing verified accounts would lose status if they did not subscribe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owner/leadership statements (Elon Musk) described prior verification as a 'lords & peasants system'; platform later introduced purchasable 'Verified Organizations' and changes to checkmark semantics (gold, grey).

rubrics_metrics.name: Official/organization verification markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter implemented a second 'Official' marker (grey tick with 'Official' text) for high-profile government and commercial entities; later replaced with a gold checkmark for organizations and a grey check mark for government and multilateral accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In March 2023 the gold check mark was made available for organizations to purchase through the Verified Organizations program (formerly Twitter Blue for Business).

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety Mode / automated harassment mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Safety Mode aims to limit unwelcome interactions through automated detection of negative engagements; authors of tweets identified as harmful or uninvited will be temporarily unable to follow, DM, or see tweets from the user with Safety Mode enabled during the temporary block period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safety Mode's technology assesses existing relationships to prevent blocking accounts that the user frequently interacts with, reducing false positives for close contacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report abuse, reporting and blocking policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter introduced a 'report abuse' button (Aug 2013) and updated reporting/blocking policies in December 2014 to handle tweets containing threats and harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies and tools evolved following public outcry; community-developed blocking mechanisms (e.g., Randi Harper's) influenced platform blocking features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content removal for images of deceased persons upon authorized request
rubrics_metrics.description: After sharing of images showing killings (e.g., James Foley in 2014), Twitter said that in certain cases it would delete pictures of people who had died after requests from family members and 'authorized individuals'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a conditional content-removal policy driven by family/authorized requests in sensitive contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension criteria for accounts promoting extremism/terrorism
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter enforced policies banning use of the platform to promote extremism; accounts promoting terrorism or coordinating abuse (multi-account evasion, brigading) are subject to suspension. Example: suspension of many accounts tied to QAnon and other groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twitter reported banning 235,000 accounts over six months (2016) and suspended 166,513 accounts for promoting terrorism in a later reporting period; enforcement examples and quantitative reporting accompany the policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policies on coordinated manipulation and multi-account abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts engaging in spammy behavior, state-linked information operations, coordinated attacks, or attempts to evade previous suspensions violate manipulation policies and may be removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twitter removed thousands of accounts attributed to state-run operations and large-scale spam; investigations may attribute groups of accounts to single operations and remove them accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: EU code of conduct content-review timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter, along with other companies, jointly agreed to a European Union code of conduct obligating them to review 'the majority of valid notifications for removal of illegal hate speech' posted on their services within 24 hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a time-to-review standard tied to EU expectations for takedown of illegal hate speech notifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account transparency labels for political candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter partnered with Ballotpedia to add special labels verifying the authenticity of political candidates running for election in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labeling aims to increase authenticity signals for civic actors and combat impersonation/misinformation during elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy practices: collection, sharing, and notification
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets are public by default, but accounts can be protected; Twitter collects personally identifiable information and shares it with third parties as specified in its privacy policy. Twitter stated it would notify users about law enforcement and governmental requests for their information unless legally prevented from doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform reserves rights described in its privacy policy (including sale of information if company changes hands); legal process (subpoenas) have prompted platform notification practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional user-servicing changes and GDPR applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2015 Twitter changed legal servicing of users outside the United States to the Ireland-based Twitter International Company, making those users subject to Irish and EU data protection laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structural change altered users' applicable privacy law and data-protection remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising-measurement opt-out change for outside-EEA users
rubrics_metrics.description: On April 8, 2020 Twitter announced that users outside of the European Economic Area or United Kingdom (thus not subject to GDPR) would no longer be allowed to opt out of sharing 'mobile app advertising measurements' to Twitter third-party partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces opt-out privacy controls for affected users and affects how advertisers can target those users.

rubrics_metrics.name: FTC enforcement and penalty for deceptive use of security data
rubrics_metrics.description: On May 25, 2022 Twitter was fined $150 million by the FTC and the US Department of Justice for collecting users' contact details used for security and using them for targeted advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedy included requirement to notify users, prohibition on profiting from deceptively collected data, and enforcement of past agreement terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of recommendation algorithm — open-source release and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: On March 31, 2023 Twitter released source code for its recommendation algorithm to GitHub to increase transparency; later updates (Jan 2026) introduced dependency on an external large language model, which researchers said made the disclosed code lack transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open-sourcing algorithmic code is presented as a transparency measure, but reliance on external black-box models can undermine that transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: API access policies and developer relations (OAuth, usage limits, paid tiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter's public API launched in 2006 and became an iconic REST API; in 2010 Twitter mandated OAuth, later introduced stricter usage limits (2012), and in Jan-Feb 2023 ended third-party access to APIs and free access, instituting paid tier plans with limited access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy changes (mandating OAuth, launching internal URL shortener, usage limits, ending free access) impacted developer trust and ecosystem; developers were given short notice in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovators Patent Agreement (defensive patent use)
rubrics_metrics.description: On April 17, 2012 Twitter announced an 'Innovators Patent Agreement' which would obligate Twitter to only use its patents for defensive purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated aim: to limit offensive patent litigation by committing patents to defensive-only deployment; the entry notes 'clarification needed' in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account-display transparency features (location, history, username changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: In November 2025 X began displaying various information on user accounts for transparency such as location, history, and username changes to combat bots and other malicious accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The platform's own rollout raised questions about the accuracy/consistency of displayed data; experts noted such displays can help detect rage-farming and foreign influence operations but may also be inconsistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and differentiation of bot accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: A bot is a computer program that can automatically tweet, retweet, and follow other accounts; benign bots may generate creative content and product updates, whereas malicious bots can amplify popularity, push products, spread misinformation, spam or slander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimates of fake accounts have varied (e.g., 20 million in 2013, a 2020 estimate at 15% of accounts). The API and cloud servers make bots feasible; detection and removal form part of moderation policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 230 safe-harbour applicability to platform liability
rubrics_metrics.description: US courts have upheld Section 230 safe harbor for Twitter, which dictates that operators of interactive computer services are not liable for the content published by their users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Amman shooting-related lawsuit alleging provision of material support to terrorist organizations was dismissed and the dismissal affirmed on appeal, citing Section 230 protections.
